name: SaaS-First
description: A pattern that prioritises adopting Software-as-a-Service products over building custom solutions. Aligned with the UK Government Cloud First policy and Technology Code of Practice, this approach reduces operational burden by leveraging commercially available platforms for common business capabilities.
whenToUse: Common business capabilities where mature SaaS products exist (CRM, HR, finance, collaboration)
Scenarios where speed to delivery is prioritised over customisation
Small teams without capacity to build and operate custom infrastructure
Non-differentiating capabilities that do not provide competitive advantage
Organisations seeking to reduce operational burden and technical debt
whenNotToUse: Unique business processes that cannot be supported by available SaaS products
Services handling SECRET or TOP SECRET data where SaaS hosting is not accredited
Scenarios requiring deep customisation that would fight against the SaaS product's design
Workloads with strict data residency requirements that SaaS providers cannot meet
Core differentiating capabilities where vendor lock-in would be strategically risky

typicalComponents.name: SaaS Platform
typicalComponents.purpose: Provide the core business capability as a managed service
typicalComponents.technology: ServiceNow, Salesforce, Microsoft 365, or domain-specific SaaS

typicalComponents.name: Identity Federation
typicalComponents.purpose: Integrate SaaS authentication with corporate identity provider
typicalComponents.technology: SAML 2.0 or OIDC federation with Azure AD or Okta

typicalComponents.name: Integration Layer
typicalComponents.purpose: Connect SaaS platform with internal systems via APIs
typicalComponents.technology: MuleSoft, Azure Logic Apps, or custom middleware

typicalComponents.name: Data Export/Backup
typicalComponents.purpose: Extract data from SaaS for backup, reporting, or migration purposes
typicalComponents.technology: Platform APIs with scheduled extraction jobs

typicalComponents.name: Governance Dashboard
typicalComponents.purpose: Monitor SaaS usage, compliance, and cost across the organisation
typicalComponents.technology: Cloud Access Security Broker (CASB) or custom reporting

securityControls: Federate authentication through corporate identity provider — no separate credentials
Implement conditional access policies (device compliance, location, MFA)
Review SaaS provider's security certifications (ISO 27001, SOC 2, Cyber Essentials Plus)
Implement data loss prevention policies for sensitive data in SaaS platforms
Conduct supply chain risk assessment per NCSC guidance
Ensure contractual data processing agreements comply with UK GDPR
resilienceConsiderations: SaaS provider manages infrastructure resilience — review their SLA commitments
Implement data export strategy to avoid vendor lock-in and enable migration
Understand the provider's disaster recovery and business continuity capabilities
Plan for provider outages — identify manual workarounds for critical processes
Maintain awareness of provider's change management and deprecation policies
costConsiderations: Subscription licensing costs per user or per feature tier
Integration development costs to connect SaaS with internal systems
Potential cost savings from eliminating custom development and operations
Consider total cost of ownership including training, customisation, and data migration
Factor in contract exit costs and data extraction effort for future migration
Volume licensing discounts through Crown Commercial Service frameworks
operationalConsiderations: Reduced operational burden — vendor manages patching, scaling, and availability
Vendor relationship management and contract governance required
Change management for SaaS updates that may affect user workflows
User training and adoption support for new SaaS platforms
Data governance must extend to SaaS-hosted data
Exit strategy must be documented in case of vendor failure or contract end

services.name: Dynamics 365
services.purpose: CRM and ERP as a service

questionsToAsk: Has a market assessment been conducted to identify suitable SaaS products?
What are the data residency and sovereignty requirements for this workload?
What is the exit strategy if the SaaS provider fails or the contract ends?
Can the SaaS product meet the required security classification without customisation?
What integrations are needed between the SaaS platform and internal systems?
Is the SaaS product available through Crown Commercial Service frameworks?
commonMistakes: Heavily customising a SaaS product to the point where upgrades become impossible
Not conducting a proper supply chain risk assessment before procurement
Failing to plan an exit strategy, creating unacceptable vendor lock-in
Choosing SaaS for a capability that requires deep customisation unique to the organisation
Not federating identity, creating credential sprawl and security gaps
